# Where this lab fits

Module 2 asks **"what varies with what?"** You now have a set of candidate need
indicators. This lab is where you actually *look* at them — their distributions,
how they relate to each other, and how they behave across geography — and then
make a defensible decision about **which ones belong in the rating** and which
are redundant or off-target. You are not building the score yet (that's next
lab); you are choosing its ingredients and writing down why.

The two habits from earlier labs still apply and are still graded:
**reproducibility** (every figure and number comes from code) and **fitness for
purpose** (an indicator that correlates with need is not automatically a good
*measure* of it).

# Get oriented

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)

d <- read_csv("data_raw/tn_tract_analysis.csv")
glimpse(d)
```

Notice two kinds of column: **rates/percents** you will analyze
(`poverty_rate`, `novehicle_rate`, `uninsured_pct`, `age65_pct`,
`disability_pct`), and the **counts behind some of them** (`poverty_count`,
`poverty_universe`, `novehicle_count`, `households`). The counts matter later.

# Build an accessibility measure from the health data

So far every indicator measures *need*. The project also needs a measure of
*service access* — and unlike the ACS columns, you build this one yourself, from
the health-center **locations**. This is the spatial half of the lab.

The idea: for each tract, how far is it to the nearest health center, and how
many are nearby? We measure from each tract's **centroid** (its center point).
Distances must be computed in a projected coordinate system measured in meters,
not in longitude/latitude — so we transform to one (EPSG:5070, a US equal-area
projection) first.

```r
tracts <- st_read("data_raw/tn_tracts.gpkg")
hc     <- st_read("data_raw/tn_health_centers.gpkg")

# Project both to meters, then take tract centroids.
tracts_m    <- st_transform(tracts, 5070)
hc_m        <- st_transform(hc, 5070)
centroids_m <- st_centroid(tracts_m)

# Distance (km) from each tract centroid to the NEAREST health center:
nearest <- st_nearest_feature(centroids_m, hc_m)
tracts$dist_nearest_km <- as.numeric(
  st_distance(centroids_m, hc_m[nearest, ], by_element = TRUE)
) / 1000

# How many centers are within 15 km of the centroid:
tracts$n_centers_15km <- lengths(
  st_is_within_distance(centroids_m, hc_m, dist = 15000)
)
```

Join the two access measures back to your data table so they sit alongside the
need indicators:

```r
access <- tracts |> st_drop_geometry() |> select(GEOID, dist_nearest_km, n_centers_15km)
d <- d |> left_join(access, by = "GEOID")
```

**Think about what this does and doesn't capture** (write a sentence — it goes in
your brief): centroid distance treats everyone in a tract as standing at its
center, which is a poor approximation in large rural tracts; and it's a
straight-line distance, not travel time on roads. A dot on a map is a location,
not a guarantee of capacity, hours, or who is served. Access is now one of your
candidate indicators, with real limitations to document.

# Distributions

Look at every candidate — need indicators **and** your new access measures —
before trusting any of it. Set the candidate list once and reuse it:

```r
candidates <- c("poverty_rate","novehicle_rate","uninsured_pct",
                "age65_pct","disability_pct","dist_nearest_km","n_centers_15km")

d |>
  select(all_of(candidates)) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "indicator", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  facet_wrap(~ indicator, scales = "free") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Concise summaries — **center, spread, and shape**:

```r
d |>
  summarise(across(
    all_of(candidates),
    list(median = ~median(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
         mean   = ~mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
         sd     = ~sd(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
         min    = ~min(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
         max    = ~max(.x, na.rm = TRUE)),
    .names = "{.col}_{.fn}"
  ))
```

**Then describe each distribution in words** — this is a graded skill, not busywork.
For each indicator write one sentence naming its **center** (typical value),
**spread** (how variable), and **shape** (roughly symmetric, right-skewed,
bimodal?), and flag any impossible or suspicious values. "Poverty rate is
right-skewed, centered near 0.15, with a long tail of high-poverty tracts" is the
kind of sentence we're looking for — not just a plot.

# Associations and redundancy

```r
# One pair, up close:
ggplot(d, aes(poverty_rate, uninsured_pct)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  theme_minimal()

# All pairs at once (need indicators AND access):
d |>
  select(all_of(candidates)) |>
  cor(use = "pairwise.complete.obs") |>
  round(2)
```

For each strongly correlated pair, decide: do they carry **distinct
information**, or is one mostly restating the other? Two indicators that are
nearly the same thing shouldn't both go into the rating with full weight.

Then look specifically at the **need-vs-access** question the project exists to
answer: do high-need tracts (say, high `poverty_rate`) also tend to have **poor**
access (high `dist_nearest_km`)? Plot it and describe the relationship in words —
this is the substantive heart of the rating.

# Map two indicators

Join to the tract geometry you already have from Lab 1 and map two indicators as
classed choropleths (reuse your Lab 1 approach).

```r
tracts <- st_read("data_raw/tn_tracts.gpkg")
tj <- tracts |> left_join(d, by = "GEOID")

ggplot(tj) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = poverty_rate), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(na.value = "grey90") +
  labs(title = "Poverty rate") + theme_minimal()
```

Where do high values cluster? Do two indicators light up the *same* places, or
different ones? Save the maps to `figures/`.

# Compare a relationship across geographic context

A relationship can differ between kinds of place. Make a simple **metro /
non-metro** split using county codes (the first 5 characters of `GEOID`), then
compare one relationship across the two groups. Tennessee's largest metro
counties include Davidson (`47037`), Shelby (`47157`), Knox (`47093`), and
Hamilton (`47065`).

```r
d <- d |>
  mutate(metro = if_else(county_geoid %in% c("47037","47157","47093","47065"),
                         "metro", "non-metro"))

d |>
  group_by(metro) |>
  summarise(cor_pov_unins = cor(poverty_rate, uninsured_pct,
                                use = "pairwise.complete.obs"))
```

Is the association the same in metro and non-metro tracts? What would it mean for
the rating if it isn't?

# Scale changes the answer: aggregate to county

Now change the spatial unit — from tract to county — and watch what happens.
Aggregate poverty to the county level the **right way**: sum the numerator and
denominator, then divide (averaging the tract rates ignores that tracts hold
different numbers of people).

```r
county <- d |>
  group_by(county_geoid) |>
  summarise(
    poverty_count    = sum(poverty_count, na.rm = TRUE),
    poverty_universe = sum(poverty_universe, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  mutate(poverty_rate_county = poverty_count / poverty_universe)
```

## First, univariately: the distribution itself changes

Compare the **distribution** of poverty at the two scales — same underlying
reality, different unit of analysis:

```r
c(tract_sd  = sd(d$poverty_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
  county_sd = sd(county$poverty_rate_county, na.rm = TRUE))
```

The county distribution is **narrower** — aggregation averages away the extremes,
so the spread shrinks and the tails compress. Plot both and describe the shift in
center/spread/shape in words. This is *spatial support*: the same quantity looks
more or less variable depending on the size of the unit you measure it on. A
"high-poverty county" hides high- and low-poverty tracts inside it.

## Then, bivariately: the relationship can change too

Compare that to the **wrong** aggregation, to see how far off averaging rates can
be:

```r
wrong <- d |>
  group_by(county_geoid) |>
  summarise(poverty_rate_avg = mean(poverty_rate, na.rm = TRUE))

county |> left_join(wrong, by = "county_geoid")
```

Compare that to the **wrong** way, and see how far apart they can be:

```r
wrong <- d |>
  group_by(county_geoid) |>
  summarise(poverty_rate_avg = mean(poverty_rate, na.rm = TRUE))

county |> left_join(wrong, by = "county_geoid")
```

Then look at a relationship at the county scale versus the tract scale (e.g.
poverty vs. another indicator) and describe how it changes. Find one **tract**
whose story disappears or reverses once it's blended into its county — that is
the **ecological fallacy / MAUP** in your own data.

One more point worth a sentence in your brief: you *cannot* correctly aggregate
`uninsured_pct`, `age65_pct`, or `disability_pct` this way, because they arrived
as pre-computed percents with no numerator/denominator. That is exactly why
transparent counts matter.

# Outliers as places, not rows

Find a few extreme tracts and ask *what place is this?*

```r
d |> slice_max(poverty_rate, n = 5)
d |> filter(total_population < 200) |> arrange(desc(poverty_rate))
```

Small-population tracts, university areas, and institutional group quarters
often produce extreme rates for reasons that have little to do with community
need. Note any you'd treat with caution.
